To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) performance is positively correlated with training data size, (2) performance is negatively correlated with the number of unique prompts in the training set, (3) performance is negatively impacted when the test set includes a prompt that was not in the training set (generalization to unseen prompts), and (4) performance is positively impacted by training on responses from multiple datasets.

(1) the performance of automated scoring systems is highly dependent on the amount and quality of training data available; (2) systems trained on a small amount of data (i.e. 100 responses) can perform well on a held-out test set when that set is drawn from a similar population; and (3) the best systems are able to generalize to a wide range of test data, even if the training data are drawn from a single source.

the number of responses needed to train a system is dependent on the quality of the responses, the number of responses, the number and type of prompts used, and the number and type (e.g., n-grams) of features used in the model.

, in general, larger training sets lead to better performance.

the amount of training data needed to achieve a given performance threshold is dependent on a number of factors including the number of prompts, the number of responses per prompt, the difficulty of the prompts and the performance threshold.
, for the datasets we studied, performance increases as more data is added to the training set, but the rate of improvement decreases as more training data is added.
